newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Tapie faces first night in jail on Monday.
newsitem.headline: France's Tapie faces first night in jail on Monday.

text.p: Bankrupt French businessman and former Marseille soccer boss Bernard Tapie faces a first night in jail on Monday unless he uses an emergency legal exit.

The ex-cabinet minister, who has expressed terror at the idea of jail, is to report on Monday evening either to La Sante prison in Paris, whose inmates include guerrilla mastermind "Carlos the Jackal", or to a jail in Douai, northern France.

Tapie's lawyer Jean-Yves Lienard said the 54-year-old former tycoon, who has previously used a barrage of appeals to stave off jail convictions for rigging soccer matches and tax fraud, was spending the weekend pondering what to do.
"It's up to him to decide what is best from him," Lienard told the Sunday newspaper Journal du Dimanche.

Tapie is meant to spend Monday night behind bars because the Supreme Court will rule on Tuesday on his final appeal against an eight-month sentence for a role in bribing players to fix a soccer match between Marseille and Valenciennes in 1993.

Under French law, convicts facing more than six months in jail have to spend the eve of a Supreme Court ruling behind bars. If the court upholds the sentence, Tapie will stay in jail and serve the rest of his term.
If the court agrees with Tapie, whose business empire once ranged from running shoes to weighing machines, he will walk free until a re-trial.
Tapie is facing a blizzard of other legal actions over his stewardship of the Marseille soccer club and his collapsed business empire. He has so far avoided prison.
His easiest way of staying out of jail -- perhaps for several weeks -- is to abandon the appeal to the Supreme Court. Simply not turning up to jail would annul the court hearing.
By scrapping the appeal, he would gain time because prosecutors in Paris, where Tapie lives, would then have to determine how and when he would serve the sentence.

Tapie, who has begun an alternative career as a film star, is hoping for a prison regime of semi-liberty under which he could spend only nights in jail while having the days free for his work as an actor.

Justice sources doubt another possibility, that the Supreme Court will put off Tuesday's ruling because of lingering doubts about whether Tapie is protected by his immunity as a deputy of the European Parliament, his last political job.

A French court last year ruled that he was ineligible for public office because he was personally bankrupt. But the European parliament itself has not yet taken any formal decision to eject him and will not do so until a herring on February 17.

If he went to jail "Bernard Tapie would be the first deputy under the Fifth Republic (from 1958) to be jailed while exercising his mandate without first having had a definitive judgment," lawyer Lienard said.

Tapie was convicted of paying Valenciennes players to lose to Marseille to ensure his players had an easy game just days before they played the European Cup Final. Marseille won the final against AC Milan by 1-0.

Apart from the conviction for rigging the game, Tapie is also appealing against a six-month conviction for tax fraud over his luxury yacht. He will also go on trial in May on suspicion of falsifying the accounts at Marseille.
